mbta_alerts.header: The platform at Jackson Square is undergoing renovations to improve safety and accessibility. Sections of the platform are unlevel, which may make it difficult for some riders to board and exit trains.

Orange Line: Service will be suspended between Oak Grove and Back Bay from August 20 - 30. Riders can use shuttles between Oak Grove and North Station, and the Green Line between North Station and Copley/Back Bay.

The stairway connecting the Jackson Square lobby and the south end of the platform is closed until winter 2026. Use the stairway at the north end of the platform. This closure is for the construction of a new stairway and a second elevator.
Littleton/Route 495 passengers can expect occasional traffic and detours when accessing the station due to the Foster Street reconstruction work.
Red Line: Shuttle buses replace service between JFK/UMass and Ashmont the weekend of September 19-20 while personnel perform critical bridge work along the Ashmont branch.
Normal boarding has resumed for all Haverhill Line trains at Greenwood and Wakefield.
Worcester Line Train 577 (7:40 PM from South Station) is operating 5-15 minutes behind schedule between Southborough and Worcester.
Orange Line: Shuttle buses will replace service between Back Bay and Forest Hills from September 10 - 14 to allow for work on the Ruggles Station Improvement Project.
Blue Line: All trains will operate on the outbound/eastbound track between Wonderland and Revere Beach the weekend of September 26 – 27, for switch work.

There is no accessible path connecting the inbound and outbound platforms at Wellesley Square Station. The existing path includes steep slopes and is long. Designs are underway to provide for a fully compliant pathway.

Green Line: No trains between North Station & Babcock St (B), Kenmore (C+D), & Heath St (E) the weekend of September 19 - 20. Use buses between Babcock, Kenmore, Heath St (Rt 39) & Copley/Back Bay. Use Orange Line between North Station & Back Bay.

Green Line C Branch:  Trains are not stopping at Brandon Hall through October 4 while accessibility upgrades are being done. Riders can board or alight at either Fairbanks St or Summit Ave, which are 0.1-0.2 miles away (or a 4- to 5-minute walk)

To accommodate renovations at Providence Station, construction barriers have been installed and the southern stairwell to Track 1 is out of service. Staircase access is available to Track 3 and Track 5.
Fitchburg Line Train 442 (7:30 PM from Wachusett) is operating 5-15 minutes behind schedule between West Concord and North Station.
Green Line E Branch: Symphony station is closed for major accessibility upgrades. Riders can use Prudential or Northeastern to access E Branch service. The station is expected to reopen in 2029.
The Wyoming Hill Mini-high platform project has begun. Passengers and local residents can expect construction vehicles and activity during the day through the Winter of 2026.
The Endicott Mini-high platform project has begun. Passengers and local residents can expect construction vehicles and activity during the day through the Winter of 2026.
The Riverside Ave entrance at Campello Station is currently closed. Passengers may continue to use the Plain St entrance.

news_revere.title: Acts of Kindness and Generosity from Odd Fellows Kearsarge Lodge of Odd Fellows 217 IOOF
news_revere.author: Journal Staff
news_revere.summary:
The Kearsarge Lodge of Odd Fellows is in Swampscott, just stone’s throw from Revere, and is the lodge of choice for many Revere residents. The Odd Fellows are widely known for their community service and generosity. Reaching out to many community events and programs to lend a hand, whether physically or financially.

This week, Kearsarge Lodge reached out to the Revere Society for Historical Preservation (RHCHP) and Revere Veteran’s Services, offering financial relief for some of their many community programs. The RSCHP offers a museum, featuring the history of Revere in many aspects, including their new exhibit Hometown Rocks. The RSCHP also has the Rumney Marsh Burial Ground under its financial responsibilities too. It takes money to keep the building in safe and attractive condition, allowing locals and visitors to enjoy our rich history.

The Revere Veteran’s Services Department covers a lot of ground for our nation’s heroes and/or their families. Offering emergency services to veterans in need, as well as guidance getting their well-deserved benefits from the state or federal agencies. Coats for veteran’s children, toys at Christmas for veteran’s children. There are many other services this department offers and more. One very important one, that affects over 100 veteran families a month, is the monthly food pantry. Volunteers make this a success every month, but what you can’t get is bags, that takes money. That’s 2 bags, per person filled with groceries, every month.

Today Kearsarge Lodge stepped up and donated 500 dollars to the RSCHP and their programs, and 800 dollars to Revere Veterans Services to purchase bags for their food program.

Donations are always accepted for bags, no matter what the amount, a little does go a long way to help a deserving veteran.

news_revere.title: Attending events with dogs
news_revere.author: Penny & Ed Cherubino
news_revere.summary:
Outdoor events can be fun to share with your pup, as long as you ensure the event is safe and comfortable for your dog and he will be a great ambassador for canines while in attendance.

Some seasonal outdoor events, like concerts and fireworks, prohibit dogs, but many of the spaces where such events are held are otherwise dog-friendly. We would never advise taking dogs to fireworks shows. The noise from the explosives and the presence of people looking up rather than paying attention to a dog in the area could spell trouble for even the calmest of canines.

However, in these same spots you may have opportunities to gather friends, a blanket, a picnic, and your dog for a relaxed evening outside.

Concerts and Movie Nights

Websites like BostonCentral.com provide updated details on events throughout the Greater Boston area. These include Free Friday Flicks at the Hatch Shell on the Charles River Esplanade, Wednesday night movies at Castle Island, and Monday nights at Time Out Market.

They also list concert series and will update these listings when the fall schedules are announced.

Markets and Festivals

Dogs on leashes are welcome at many farmers markets and local festivals. Always check the rules before you arrive. There is a perception that farmers’ markets close down when school begins, but many operate into October and some until Thanksgiving week. For example, the Boston Seaport Summer Market runs through October 10th.

Boston artists and craftspeople will display their work during the Boston Arts Festival at the Christopher Columbus Waterfront Park in mid-September. In addition, October will bring the spirit of Oktoberfest to beer gardens and other sites in the area. Halloween displays and costume parties will follow.

You will also find event listings on the websites of specific hosting locations. Check out the Rose Kennedy Greenway events and activities that continue through early fall:

Is This Right for Your Dog?

Here are a few tips to make these outings more enjoyable for you, your pup, and the people around you. Obviously, if your dog is not well-mannered or not comfortable around either people or dogs, this is not the right activity for you.

• If you have a high-energy dog, make sure she’s tired before the event.

• At a concert, find a spot away from speakers and watch your pup’s expression to see if the amplified sound is causing any discomfort.

• Bring water for your dog. And stash a few treats in your pocket to reward good behavior.

• Make sure your pup has plenty of opportunities to relieve himself away from the crowd to avoid an embarrassing leg lift on a neighbor’s chair.

• Don’t let your canine companion give all dogs a bad name by begging for or stealing your neighbor’s lunch.

• Tick reports are plentiful this year. Be sure to check yourself and your dog for ticks during and after the event.

Catch Up with Friends and Neighbors

news_revere.title: Zoning subcommittee tables North Shore Road towing permit request
news_revere.author: Adam Swift
news_revere.summary:
A proposed North Shore Road towing business has a month to get any potential issues cleared up and to meet with abutters before coming back to the city council's zoning subcommittee for a special permit hearing on Sept. 14.

The owners and attorney of 128 Towing and Recovery at 855 North Shore Road appeared before the subcommittee at its meeting last week for its special permit.

However, several city councillors said they had issues with 128 Towing continuing to operate at the North Shore Road location without the permit. There were also questions raised about the business and its impact on traffic and abutters from when the proposal first appeared before the council earlier this summer.

Attorney Niles Welch, representing the towing company, said he was recently retained by the owners and understood there were some issues with work being done at the site before a special permit was obtained from the city council.

“I would like to acknowledge, in speaking with my clients, that they did a lot of things backwards in applying for this permit and as any small business owner, as I can attest, this was not an intentional thing,” said Welch.

Welch said the owners, who are Revere residents, went forward with getting the business ready to operate before meeting with the ward councillor and applying for the special permit to operate.

“They only want to do the right thing, but now they are faced with the impossible situation that they are not licensed to operate a business, but they are semi-operating a business here in Revere,” said Welch. “We are here to acknowledge that is the case. In the past 48 hours, I have had some very productive conversations with members of the city, I’ve spoken with the ward councillor, I’ve had some very productive conversations with her in an effort to get in front and try to deal with some of the issues that were presented at the last city council meeting.”

Welch said the applicant was looking to table the subcommittee meeting in order to meet with abutters and residents and clear up any issues before the next zoning subcommittee meeting on Sept. 14.

However, several councillors, including Ward 5 Councillor Angela Guarino-Sawaya, said the issues went beyond needing to meet with neighbors.

Both Guarino-Sawaya and subcommittee Chair Marc Silvestri noted that the business has continued to operate without a special permit on North Shore Road after the owners were expressly told not to operate at the council meeting earlier this summer.

“We don’t want to impact the lives of anyone trying to start a small business here in Revere,” said Silvestri. “The last time they came before us, there were conditions and we spoke about not operating at this premises while they were in the process.”

However, Silvestri said he was driving by the property near the end of July and saw a flatbed truck on the site with its lights on and a driver inside.

Guarino-Sawaya said there have also been issues with neighbors seeing business being done on the site and trucks blocking traffic and the roadways.

“The neighbors behind them and across the street, they constantly call me, I guess they got into an altercation with a neighbor this past weekend because of the noise they heard,” she said.

Based on inconsistencies in the application and the resident complaints, Guarino-Sawaya said she could not allow the business in the neighborhood at this time.

“It is like he is lying right to my face, I don’t know if he is not doing it purposefully and it's just a miscommunication,” she said. “I have nothing against (the owner), I just can’t see this operation being approved with him doing everything wrong to begin with.”

Welch did raise the issue of a potential conflict of interest for Guarino-Sawaya, since two of her relatives work for a competing towing company in the city.

Guarino-Sawaya said she contacted the state ethics commission and that they advised her that she could be involved with the hearing process. She noted that her husband works part-time driving a rolloff truck for another company, and that her son works in sales for the company, but that neither of them are involved in towing, or that she would have any financial interest in the ruling.

Council President Anthony Zambuto and Councillor-at-Large Michelle Kelley both asked if there was a way the city and the business could find a compromise on the issue.

Silvestri tabled the special permit hearing until the Sept. 14 zoning subcommittee meeting to give the business and the attorney time to settle any outstanding issues. However, he said that the business cannot operate in any fashion on the property before that date.

news_revere.title: State grant will help Revere address flooding issues
news_revere.author: Adam Swift
news_revere.summary:
A nearly $100,000 state grant could help Revere residents elevate critical utilities in flood-prone basements.

Last week, Governor Maura Healey’s administration announced more than $45 million in grants to support 97 projects that will help communities across Massachusetts better withstand flooding, extreme heat, coastal erosion, and other climate impacts.

The grants were awarded through the Executive Office of Energy and Environmental Affairs’ (EEA’s) new Environment & Climate (ECO) One Stop program. The aim of the program is to help strengthen infrastructure, restore and enhance natural resources, and improve public safety while making it easier to access state funding for climate resilience projects.

In Revere, the $98,360 grant will be used to help evaluate the feasibility of developing a Utility Elevation Assistance Program to help residents elevate critical utilities (e.g., HVAC equipment, electrical panels and boilers) currently in flood-prone basements. The project will establish recommended Design Flood Elevations, identify retrofit strategies, and assess program design approaches, including eligibility criteria, administrative structures, benefit-cost evaluations, and funding mechanisms.

“Flooding in Revere’s low-lying neighborhoods frequently damages HVAC equipment, electrical panels, and boilers located in basements,” said Tom Skwierawski, the city’s director of Planning and Community Development. “This project will develop a municipal program to help residents elevate vulnerable utilities and reduce damage during future storms.”

The project will evaluate approaches to program design and funding to ensure residents can access assistance, according to Skwierawski.

“Technical analysis will identify recommended retrofit methods, establish design flood elevations for utilities, and develop planning-level cost estimates,” he said. “Community engagement will help identify potential pilot participants and inform program design. Results will provide the City with a roadmap for implementing a household-level resilience program that reduces flood impacts and strengthens community resilience.”

In announcing the statewide grants in Salem last week, Healey said the state needs infrastructure that can withstand flooding, extreme heat and severe storms.

“This $45 million investment will help communities protect residents, strengthen roads, dams, coastlines and other critical infrastructure and lower costs,” said Healey. “ECO One Stop is making it faster and easier for communities to access the funding they need to get these important projects moving.”

The inaugural ECO One Stop pilot round includes seven state grant programs supporting projects that reduce climate risks and strengthen communities, including Municipal Vulnerability Preparedness (MVP) Action, Dam & Seawall Repair or Removal, Coastal Resilience, Coastal Habitat and Water Quality, Cooling Corridors, Culvert Replacement Municipal Assistance, Culvert Replacement Training Site, and Planning Assistance. A total of 97 projects received awards, including 71 municipal projects, 14 regional planning agencies, seven nonprofit organizations, two Tribes, and three other public entities.

“We’ve seen firsthand this summer how heavy, sudden rainfall can overwhelm aging dams and culverts, how extreme heat can harm vulnerable populations, and how storms can drive bacteria to our beaches and strain our wastewater systems,” said EEA Secretary Rebecca Tepper. “The ECO One Stop program combines the power of many of the state’s major environmental grant programs in one place, so municipalities can act quickly and think creatively about how to invest in their communities. Through this investment, we’re making sure that water has a safe place to go during downpours, that communities can cool down when temperatures rise, and that our most treasured natural resources are preserved for generations to come.”

news_revere.title: Disabilities Commission holds monthly meeting
news_revere.author: Journal Staff
news_revere.summary:
The Revere Commission on Disabilities (COD) held its regular monthly meeting last Tuesday, August 11, via Zoom. On hand for the session were chair Ralph DeCicco, vice-chair Pauline Perno, Jason Barone-Cichocki, and Mario Grimanis.

Perno provided an update regarding the Revere Beach crossing safety concerns. The commission has sent a letter to State Rep. Jeff Turco and has spoken with city officials about the problem. However, Perno said she has heard nothing back.

Perno and DeCicco provided a list of the vendors and agencies that were slated to come to the third annual All Ability Beach Day at Revere Beach, which was scheduled to take place this past Saturday, August 15.

Save the Harbor/Save the Bay once again awarded a grant to the COD that provided the funding for the All Ability Day, which is being held in conjunction with the Revere Rec. Dept.

DeCicco gave a report of the July meeting of CODA (Commissions on Disabilities Alliance) that was held on July 1. He said the representative from the Newburyport COD mentioned that they will be working on their COD page on the town's website.

He noted that the Newton COD rep mentioned that they were scheduled to have a Disability Pride event on July 19.

He also said that the Boston COD representative stated that they have created a letter to send to Secretary of State William Galvin regarding the issues with the Automark voting machines and gave reasons for why they need to be replaced.

DeCicco said there were no items received from the Massachusetts Architectural Access Board (MAAB) during the month for local variances. He also noted that there was no business pertaining to Chapter 40, Section 22 handicapped parking funds.

DeCicco at the end of the meeting brought up that the commission often receives queries about housing, noting that the COD has no direct connection to housing resources.

Perno concluded the meeting by reading the COD's monthly reminder:

The Commission on Disabilities office number is 781-286-8267. Residents can also call Revere 311 directly and speak to their staff Monday through Friday. They will answer most questions, but if they are unable to assist you or if you prefer to talk with the commission directly, please ask to be transferred to the Commission on Disability direct number. Please leave a detailed message, and we will respond to you shortly.

As always, please don't hesitate to contact us if you would like to discuss or add something to our monthly meeting agenda. You can also let us know if you want to discuss any concerns. The commission is here to help and assist all residents with disabilities and their families in Revere.

The next meeting of the COD (via Zoom) is set for Tuesday evening, September 8.

news_revere.title: AHTF approves application for mortgage buy-down program, senior home repair funds
news_revere.author: Journal Staff
news_revere.summary:
The Board of Trustees of the City of Revere's Affordable Housing Trust Fund (AHTF) held its regular monthly meeting last Wednesday evening, August 12, in the City Council Chamber. On hand for the session were chair Joseph Gravellese, Treasurer Anayo Osueke, and fellow board members Dean Harris, Matt Wolfer, Laila Pietri, Lori Manzo, Deb Frank, and Judy Gosselin.

Osueke presented the treasurer's report. He said the AHTF has a balance in its account of $998,999.02. which includes $3809.55 received in interest from the past month.

The members discussed the final draft of the application for the buy-down assistance program for first-time home buyers that the AHTF has been working on for the past few months.

The program will provide financial assistance that will help persons to buy homes that they otherwise would be unable to afford. The program is designed to benefit those with incomes ranging from 60-120% of the Area Median Income (AMI).

The property will be deed-restricted. If the homeowner sells the home within 10 years, the homeowner will have to resell the property at the then-affordable price level. If the homeowner sells the property between 10 and 20 years afterwards, any profits will be split between the homeowner and the AHTF. After 20 years, the homeowner will be able to sell the property without any restrictions and keep all of the profits.

In order to be eligible, applicants must either be a resident of Revere for at least two years, or have a child in the local schools, or be a full-time (30 hours or more) employee of a Revere-based employer.

Osueke suggested some tweaks to the application regarding the requirements of the program and Gravallese said he would incorporate Osueke's suggestions before the application went "live" on the city's website.

Gravallese also said that October 21 will be the opening date for the application process with a closing date of February 3 (unless the available funds in the program are expended before that date). Those who have been approved for funding them will have until May 3 to avail themselves of the funding; otherwise, the funds will revert back to the AHTF.

The board unanimously agreed to the final form of the application and the time-line. The members then discussed how to get the word out to the community, including banks and realtors, by means of press releases, social media, and flyers.

The members next discussed renewing the Senior Citizen Home Repair program, which last year assisted 12 Revere senior homeowners with grants that totaled $50,000 (with a maximum of $5000 per grantee).

The members voted unanimously in favor of another round for the program for the coming years, increasing both the total to $85,000 and the maximum per recipient to $6000. Funds will be awarded on a first-come, first-served basis for those with completed applications.

There will be a Q&A session for prospective applicants at the Senior Center on Wednesday, August 31. The application process will open on September 8, continuing until the funds are exhausted.

Gravallese ended the meeting by announcing that the AHTF's down payment assistance program provided $10,000 each to 13 new homebuyers over the past year. This program had $150,000 available, leaving a balance of $20,000.

Gravallese suggested that the AHTF contribute another $50,000 to the program, which would make $70,000 available to prospective home-buyers for the coming year. The board voted unanimously to do so.

news_revere.title: Suffolk County DA Kevin Hayden  is proud of his many accomplishments
news_revere.author: Cary Shuman
news_revere.summary:
When Suffolk County District Attorney Kevin Hayden was introduced at a recent political event in Revere, the applause was substantial.

Mayor Patrick Keefe praised Hayden in his remarks, stating, “We’re here to celebrate our public safety. We have the most sworn officers, police and fire, that we’ve had in over two decades. We haven’t had a homicide in the City of Revere in over four years.”

A week later at an event in Chelsea, residents gave Hayden an equally enthusiastic and respectful welcome as City Councilors Leo Robinson and Calvin T. Brown hailed the district attorney’s many accomplishments during his four-plus years in office.

“Kevin Hayden has done a tremendous job working with our law enforcement officials in protecting our residents and engaging with our community,” said Robinson. “He has been highly visible at events promoting public safety and his office has always been accessible and professional in its immediate response to correspondences and phone calls from our residents. He always has a team present at such events as National Night Out and public meetings.”

Hayden, who is seeking a second term as district attorney for Suffolk Country that encompasses Boston, Revere, Winthrop, and Chelsea, said, “We have accomplished a lot of things in the short time that I’ve been in office, and we need to make sure that good work continues.”

Statistics indicate that there has been a significant decline in incidents of crime across the county that has 800,000 residents.

“Historically low crime rates don’t happen by accident, and a lot of what we’ve done over the course of the first term has helped achieve that,” said Hayden, a graduate of Dartmouth College and Boston University Law School. “Whether that’s dealing with our Juvenile Alternative Resolution (JAR) Program helping our young people and keeping them away from our criminal legal system – a program which we’ve expanded to emerging adults – it has been extraordinarily successful so far.”

Services Over Sentences (SOS), an alternative-to-prosecution program launched in 2022 by Hayden, has been a focus of the DA’s office in addressing the opioid crisis.

“The opioid epidemic continues to be a problem for us, particularly in our South End neighborhood right now, and our focus is on recovery, on getting people we call high-risk, high need, into the treatment that they need, the housing access that they need, and to give them the opportunity to build a life that they need, and hopefully, first and foremost, to get clean and sober. That’s how we address that problem. That way we can prosecute people less, and it saves lives – we have real proof of having saved lives through our Services Over Sentences program.”

Speaking about the intervention and prevention aspects of his office, Hayden, who oversees approximately 165 attorneys and 310 staff members overall, noted, “We have our Fraud Fighters piece, which is primarily geared toward our elder community, but as time goes on, we’re finding that our younger folks are very interested in it as well. When you talk about online fraud, phone scams, and the things that are happening now, particularly in this new age of AI, it’s a rampant problem. It’s one that’s hard to prosecute, so we know and we’ve learned that intervention and prevention are our most useful way of combating that problem, telling people exactly what scammers are doing, and staying up-to-date and one step ahead of them, and letting our communities know how they can prevent themselves from being defrauded.”

Hayden said that retail theft continues to be “a real issue.”

“The reality is there is no one-size-fits-all solution in how you tackle that problem,” said Hayden. “Someone who’s homeless and down and out, and starving for food who is stealing is a lot different than someone who’s running out of a store with thousands of dollars of merchandise at a time and doing that for a profit. So, we have partnered with our retailers and with law enforcement to make sure we are dealing with shoplifting and retail theft in a comprehensive and effective way.”

Hayden emphasized that his office “will always focus on the most serious and most violent crimes, first and foremost.”

“That’s what keeps people up at night, that’s what people are concerned about – everyone wants and deserves to be safe,” said Hayden. “And we continue to focus on violent crime, and how to drive it down, and how to be better. But we’re doing very well in that area. We are seeing historically low crime rates across the board.”

Hayden smiled when he was asked about the rousing receptions he has garnered at local events. He knows that there is work still to be done.

“I’m just extraordinarily humbled by the response I’ve received in our communities – it’s humbling to know that people have the confidence in my staff and me and the work we’re doing,” said Hayden. “I’m proud of the work we’ve done during my term. Rome doesn’t get built in a day. It takes time to establish things that we’ve established – the extraordinary successes across every major area. We’ve also improved the office internally as well, from a professional development standpoint, from raising the salary of our assistant district attorneys and all our staff. We’ve been able to work very closely with our legislature to get salaries increased for our staff – that’s very important when it comes to retention and being able to keep people around. And we’ve also increased the number of staff. We have 40 more people working in the office than we had before, and we continue to work on adding some more, because if you don’t have the people to do the work, then it’s hard to get it done. I’m so proud of the work we’ve done. We have some of the best public servants in the entire state doing this work. We’re proud of what we’re doing in Suffolk County, keeping our communities safe while also continuing to advance important ideas around criminal and legal reform. But we’re not resting on our laurels.”

news_revere.title: New teachers begin their RPS journey with orientation week
news_revere.author: Special to the Journal
news_revere.summary:
Revere Public Schools welcomed new teachers last week as educators gathered for New Teacher Orientation, an annual program designed to introduce new staff members to the district, its schools, and the community they will soon serve.

The orientation, facilitated by RPS educators Matt Costa, Christina Porter, Nancy Martel, Ann McLaughlin, Rick Norris, Michelle Vail, and Jill Foley, provides new teachers with an opportunity to become familiar with the district before students return for the first day of school on Aug. 25. Throughout the week, the new educators are taking part in professional development and training while learning about district resources, expectations, programs, and the diverse community that makes up Revere Public Schools.

The week kicked off last Monday with a welcome from Assistant Superintendents Dr. Richard Gallucci, Dr. Danielle Mokaba-Bernardo, and Dr. Lourenço Garcia. Each spoke about the excitement surrounding the arrival of a new group of educators and the important role they will play in the lives of Revere students and families.

The assistant superintendents encouraged the new teachers to view their arrival not simply as the beginning of a new job but as the start of a journey within RPS. They spoke about the collaborative culture of the district and the opportunity educators have to grow professionally while building meaningful relationships with students, colleagues, and families.

Gallucci also highlighted the supports available to educators throughout the district, emphasizing that new teachers are not expected to navigate their first year in Revere alone. From school-based colleagues and administrators to mentoring, professional development, and district-level resources, RPS has developed a network of supports designed to help educators grow, succeed, and thrive.

That support begins during orientation. In addition to training and professional development, the week allows new teachers to learn more about Revere itself—an important part of understanding the students and families they will serve. The district’s mentoring program will continue that work throughout the school year, connecting new educators with experienced colleagues who can provide guidance and support as they settle into their classrooms.

For Costa, Porter, Martel, McLaughlin, Norris, Vail, and Foley, New Teacher Orientation is also an opportunity to begin building connections among educators who may work in different schools and grade levels but are beginning their RPS experience together. Those relationships can become an important support network as teachers move through their first year in the district.

With the opening of school just weeks away, the new teachers will soon transition from orientation and preparation to their individual schools and classrooms, where they will meet their colleagues, students, and families.

RPS continues to recruit candidates for several remaining vacancies ahead of the new school year, with many of the openings concentrated in special education and English as a second language positions. Qualified educators interested in joining Revere Public Schools can view current openings and apply through the employment portal.

For this week’s newest educators, however, the hiring process is complete, and a new chapter is beginning — one that will officially get underway when Revere students return to classrooms on Aug. 25.

news_revere.title: District's new identity draws inspiration from Revere Junior Patriots While creating a unified brand for RPS Athletics
news_revere.author: Special to the Journal
news_revere.summary:
As Revere Public Schools prepares for the future—including the opening of its new high school—the district has unveiled an official Patriot logo that will serve as the unified symbol of Revere athletics and school spirit.

The logo was formally introduced during July’s Revere School Committee meeting, capping nearly a year of collaboration among administrators, educators, students, and community members to create a single, recognizable identity for the district.

The effort began last fall when Revere High School physical education teacher Keith Correia approached Athletic Director Frank Shea and Superintendent Dr. Dianne Kelly with a simple but important idea: Revere needed one official Patriot logo.

At the time, multiple versions of the Patriot mascot were being used across uniforms, publications, and promotional materials, creating an inconsistent visual identity for the district.

“His reasoning was we had three or four images that were floating around that different groups would use,” Shea explained during his presentation to the school committee. “He thought it was a good idea, going into a new high school, to have one solid logo that would be on uniforms and paper correspondence.”

Dr. Kelly asked Shea to lead the project, assembling a committee representing athletics, academics, administration, the arts, and the broader community.

The committee included Shea; Michael Hinojosa, director of Parks and Recreation; Julianne Falzarano, Revere High School vice principal and former cheerleading coach; Jill Foley, director of health and wellness; Keith Correia, physical education teacher; Michael Flynn, teacher, cross-country coach, and tennis coach; Kepler Celamy, senior class president; Harley Dijon, AP Art and Design student; and Sovannita Va, art student and Art Club member.

Over the course of five meetings throughout the school year, the committee refined its vision for the next generation of Revere athletics.

As the vision began to take shape, committee members drew inspiration from the logo of the Revere Junior Patriots Youth Football and Cheer organization, which has been familiar to generations of young Revere athletes.

The Junior Patriots have long introduced some of Revere’s youngest athletes to the city’s football and cheer traditions, making their Patriot imagery a natural point of inspiration as RPS considered a new identity for its own athletic programs. Rather than simply adopting the existing image, however, students and committee members used elements of the Junior Patriots’ Patriot as a starting point. They developed a new design specifically for Revere Public Schools.

Shea acknowledged that connection during the unveiling, noting that the new RPS logo “has some similarity to the Revere Junior Patriot logo” and that students took “a little bit of that image” before redesigning the Patriot’s hat, face, and other features.

The result creates a visual connection between the youth programs where many Revere children are first introduced to athletics and the school teams they may one day represent, while giving RPS a distinct identity.

After establishing the overall direction during the first several meetings, committee members began translating those ideas into a finished design. Shea credited both Foley and student artist Sovannita Va for helping shape the final product through numerous revisions.

“When we had all the edits, Miss Va was tremendous with changing things, moving things around, giving us new images,” Shea said. “She was a great help.”

The finished logo pays homage to both Revere’s athletic tradition and its youth sports community while giving the Patriot a more modern, distinctive appearance. The committee redesigned the character’s face and iconic tricorn hat, building upon that familiar hometown imagery to create something unique to Revere Public Schools.

The logo also incorporates another tribute to hometown pride. The outline of the Patriot’s face forms the shape of the Commonwealth of Massachusetts, an element designed and inspired by the Junior Patriots’ logo, complete with a star marking Revere’s location—a detail highlighted by Mayor Patrick Keefe during the unveiling.

“If you didn’t notice, the logo features the outline of Massachusetts with a star indicating Revere’s location inscribed on the Patriot’s face,” Keefe told those in attendance. “So, it’s pretty cool. Very, very, very talented.”

The design was displayed on screen for School Committee members and viewers watching from home, providing a closer look at the Massachusetts outline and other details incorporated into the new Patriot.

Beyond serving as the official athletic mark, the new logo represents a broader effort to strengthen the district’s identity as Revere enters a new chapter with the construction of its new high school campus.

Shea said he hopes the logo quickly becomes a symbol students and alumni rally around.

“We’re proud that this will be our logo moving forward,” he said. “I can’t wait to see it on some new uniforms.”

Mayor Keefe echoed that excitement, adding that he already envisions the new Patriot coming to life at athletic events.

“I’m looking forward to seeing the physical mascot with the hat wearing the new uniform, running up and down the sidelines or in the field house,” the mayor said.

The collaborative design process also reflects the district’s commitment to including student voices in projects that shape the future of Revere Public Schools. By including student artists in the logo’s design, the committee made sure the new Patriot was not simply made for students but was shaped by students themselves.

It also creates a fitting bridge between generations of Revere athletes—from children who first put on a uniform with the Junior Patriots Youth Football and Cheer organization to the student-athletes who proudly represent Revere Public Schools at the high school level.

Beginning with this school year, Revere athletics and school spirit will have a new official visual identity. The new Patriot logo will be featured on uniforms, athletic wear, publications, signage, and promotional materials throughout the district. As students, staff, and alumni look forward to a new era of Revere Public Schools, the redesigned Patriot will serve as an enduring emblem of unity, tradition, and hometown pride.

news_revere.title: What the Flock?
news_revere.author: Kane Dimasso-Scott
news_revere.summary:
What the Flock?

Dear Editor,

You’ve probably heard about the latest “automatic license plate readers (ALPRs),” Flock, in the news nationwide lately as they have been getting some much-deserved bad press over their invasive privacy practices. What you might not have heard is that there are already a handful operating in Revere. They are constantly gathering data and building a profile of the residents and their movements.

While they have been installed under the guise of ALPRs, to improve public safety, they are so much more insidious than that. Across the nation, we’ve seen these systems misused, and the police cannot guarantee our data isn’t being accessed by individuals outside of our community. Furthermore, recent municipal studies show these cameras are incredibly fallible, with some cities reporting an alarming 71% misread and failure rate on license plate alerts. This makes the system far too unreliable and untrustworthy to be operated in our community.

The police chief will be appearing at the Revere City Council meeting on Aug. 24 at 6 p.m. to answer questions about the Flock cameras. I highly encourage the public to attend and voice their concerns.

Kane DiMasso-Scott

UPDATE:

After press time, we received word that Chief LaVita will not be able to attend the Aug. 24 council meeting. She is planning to attend the following Council meeting in September to answer questions from the public regarding the Flock ALPR cameras in Revere.

news_revere.title: More than a check up: The vital role of annual well-child visits
news_revere.author: Dr. Ana Stankovic
news_revere.summary:
As families prepare for the upcoming school year, many are focused on school supplies, schedules and getting back into routines. But one of the most important back-to-school steps happens before the first day of class: scheduling a well-child visit.

Because many pediatric and family practice schedules often fill quickly throughout the summer, now is an ideal time for parents to make appointments. These preventive visits help ensure children and adolescents are ready for the year ahead, not only academically, but physically, emotionally and developmentally.

What is a well-child visit?

Well-child visits are annual preventive appointments with a pediatrician or family medicine provider. Sometimes referred to as physicals, these visits help track a child’s overall health and development, including:

• Growth and developmental milestones

• Immunizations and preventive screenings

• Vision and hearing checks

• Emotional and behavioral health

Beyond these clinical measures, well-child visits also give parents a chance to complete school or sports forms and raise any concerns before the school year begins. More importantly, they create dedicated time for families and providers to discuss a child’s overall wellbeing, connecting physical health with emotional wellness and any developmental concerns that may affect success in school and at home.

Mental health is part of overall health

The broader view of a checkup may be especially important when it comes to mental health. A child’s emotional wellbeing may be closely linked to their physical health. According to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), approximately 1 in 5 children ages 3 to 17 in the US has a diagnosable mental, emotional or behavioral disorder. Mental health needs can look different depending on age and stage of development.

Young children may experience separation anxiety or behavioral outbursts. School-age children may struggle with focus, stress or social challenges. Teens may show changes in mood, sleep or engagement. While many of these changes are a normal part of growing up, they can also signal when additional support may be needed.

The good news is that early conversations with a pediatrician can make a difference. A well-child visit is a natural time to check in and help children understand that it’s okay to talk about how they’re feeling. These conversations may also help normalize emotional health as an essential part of routine care.

To help support these conversations and preventive care visits, families are encouraged to review their health plan benefits and available resources as many plans include behavioral health support and programs like Child & Family Behavioral Coaching, which may help families navigate everyday emotional and behavioral challenges.

The importance of dental & vision care

Don’t forget to take advantage of vision and dental benefits to help make sure kiddos are ready to learn.

Vision benefits may include annual eye exams that can detect changes in eyesight that may affect learning in the classroom. More than 600,000 children and teens in the U.S. suffer from some form of vision loss.1 School-based screenings are valuable but may not detect more complex issues. Annual comprehensive eye exams are recommended throughout the school years.

Dental benefits may include routine cleanings and exams that help catch concerns before they become more serious. Tooth decay, or cavities, is one of the most common chronic diseases among children and may contribute to missed days at school.1 Help monitor teeth and gum health with dental exams twice a year. Ensure your children are brushing for 2 minutes twice a day and flossing daily.

Don’t forget a healthy diet

Proper nutrition is essential when it comes to supporting your child’s physical and emotional health, plus their growth and development.1 That includes meals with a variety of vegetables, whole fruits, grains, dairy and proteins. It’s best to avoid foods high in added sugars, saturated fats and sodium.

Scheduling a well-child visit is a simple but important step that gives families the opportunity to address concerns support a child’s overall wellbeing throughout the year.

Dr. Ana Stankovic is the Chief Medical Officer for UnitedHealthcare of New England.

news_revere.title: Why I’m running for 6th District Governor’s Council
news_revere.author: Diann Baylis
news_revere.summary:
As we approach the September 1st Democratic Primary, I wanted to share with voters why I decided to run to be your next Governor’s Councilor. As I’ve traveled across the 20 communities that make up our Governor’s Council district (which stretches from Marblehead to Somerville), the first question I get when I talk with voters is, what is the Governor’s Council?

It’s the right question to ask. The Governor’s Council is the elected body in Massachusetts that confirms judicial nominations made by the Governor, at every level of our courts, including the Supreme Judicial Court (the Governor’s Council also confirms nominees to the Parole Board, notaries public and justices of the peace, and they play an important role in our elections).

I decided to run for Governor’s Council for three main reasons.

First, as an immigration attorney, I represent immigrant children as they seek a special juvenile visa that starts in the probate court (not in the federal immigration courts). I have dealt with probate judges that are not being open minded to these kids’ unique circumstances and as a result are delaying their progress, leaving them vulnerable to deportation. I want to better vet and educate these judges, so that we can streamline this process and protect immigrant kids.

Second, in my past work as a family law attorney, including as a pro bono attorney for the “Lawyer of the Day” program at the Essex Probate Court, I have supported women and children in proceedings involving restraining orders, divorce, custody, and child support. I have seen first-hand the sometimes arbitrary decisions that probate judges make, that fundamentally affect the lives and safety of women, children and families. I have seen women and children who would show up in desperate need of the court’s services but were very wary to face a judge without some support which we provided. I want to make sure they are dealing with judges that will show fairness and compassion.

The third reason is that I want to make sure, as a lifelong Democrat, that every vote is counted and that our democracy is protected and preserved for future generations. The Governor’s Council is the body that certifies state election results before they are considered final. In the current political climate, with democracy under threat, this role could become vitally important.

As your Governor’s Councilor I ultimately want to make sure that judges that are nominated are not only educated but also open-minded, with integrity and compassion. I have travelled to all 20 communities in this Governor’s Council district and have talked to many residents who share the same concerns as I do. I will represent these views as your representative on the Governor’s Council.

Please vote by mail, vote early, or vote in person on September 1st, but I am asking for your vote in the Democratic primary. Learn more on my campaign website at https://www.votefordiann.com.

Diann Baylis is an immigration attorney, and a candidate for Governor’s Council in the 6th Governor’s Council District.

news_revere.title: Justice beyond the headlines: why I’m voting for Kevin Hayden
news_revere.author: Senator Lydia Edwards
news_revere.summary:
September 1, 2026 is primary election day. With only Democrats running for Suffolk County District Attorney, the race will be over in September rather than in November. We have a choice to make this year, and unlike most seats that are up for reelection, District Attorney Kevin Hayden is being challenged seemingly from his left (Rachael Rollins) and his right (Linda Champion).

I have been an attorney in Massachusetts for 20 years this November. Today, I serve as the state senator for Boston, Revere and Winthrop (three of the four towns in Suffolk County). I am also Senate Chair of the Judiciary Committee and now as the legislative session has come to an end, I am serving as a bar advocate (criminal defense attorney) for people that cannot afford private attorneys. Finally, I am an adjunct law professor at Suffolk Law School and in my spare time I am a Judge Advocate General (military attorney) in the Massachusetts Army National Guard.

I want to first acknowledge that I have endorsed both Rollins (2018) and Hayden (2022) for District Attorney of Suffolk County. I have written op eds about both acknowledging their work and dedication to the people of Suffolk County. I have excitedly defended them both and enjoyed their endorsements and support. I even wrote a letter of support for Rollins’ appointment to be U.S. Attorney. I know them both personally and professionally. I have spoken to Ms. Champion less so but did meet with her while she was running for District Attorney in 2018.

I lead with all the above background experience and political decisions to state, unequivocally, that District Attorney Kevin Hayden should be resoundingly re-elected. It is not just politics for me, it is my profession and it is personal.

Let’s talk about his qualifications. Kevin has dedicated decades of his life to community representation. He worked his way up from a young Assistant District Attorney to his appointment as District Attorney. It’s true, he didn’t run initially for this office – Governor Baker had to find a qualified public servant to replace then District Attorney Rollins when Rollins left to become the U.S. Attorney. Since starting his position as DA, Kevin has proven publicly what so many people know of him personally: he just wants to do the work. He is not flashy. You won’t find him tweeting tirades, he doesn’t come with the quick comebacks and he doesn’t play politics.

That is why we need him. If there is anything we are growing tired of its prosecution and advocacy by clicks and social media. The real work doesn’t happen on screen most of the time – it’s in the moments of crisis, it’s holding the surviving loved ones, it’s praying for the safe return of people who are missing, it’s house calls. Kevin does all of that. Kevin genuinely leads with his heart and most of that work is unseen.

It’s easy to judge a district attorney, or abandon one, when you don’t like the decisions they make. To bring charges against a police officer (who is innocent until proven guilty) was a difficult decision that only a district attorney can make with discernment. While some may like or may not like the decision, I don’t think there is one person that can say Kevin did it due to politics or to curry favor with the police. I would argue the same when it comes to his choice to prosecute crimes that Rollins chose to ignore. He isn’t making political decisions. He is making prosecutorial ones based on what is best for public trust and public safety.

That’s what I want in my district attorney – to just do the job – and we are getting more than that with Kevin. He has creatively approached public safety and continued programs that worked to keep people out of jail and communities safe. Fundamentally, Kevin is a man of deep faith and believes that people deserve a second chance. He supported eviction record sealing knowing that housing stability was fundamental to recovery and recovery was fundamental to staying out of jail. Kevin expanded the Services Over Sentencing program with $400,000 of seized drug money because “traditional court involvement is not the answer for many of the vulnerable individuals in the center or fringes of Mass and Cass. We need to present alternative solutions that identify and address the issues that brought them there in the first place…, and… money seized from drug-related convictions is a fitting method to fund it.”

Another example is Hayden’s new initiative for young adults. While Beacon Hill is deciding whether to raise the age for court involved youth to 18 years for Juvenile Court, Hayden already piloted a program. Hayden’s Emerging Adult Program follows science and creates “diversionary pathways to prosecution for emerging adults, (18-25 years old) connecting them with established non-profit organizations like ROCA to create individualized service plans in conjunction with an ongoing criminal case. The program is in 4 phases and can last 6 to 18 months during which participants meet with wrap-around services, are held accountable for their mistakes and hopefully graduate with a clean record. That is justice centered prosecution. It is also community focused accountability that allows the young person to earn a new beginning and the community to heal.

My final example (though there are many more) of Hayden’s justice centered prosecution is his recent support and contributions to the Protect Act. This new law protects court houses, schools, and hospitals from ICE (Immigration Enforcement). For District Attorney Hayden that means prosecutions of defendants won’t be interrupted by federal agents. It means victims and witnesses will come to court and testify without fear of being detained. It means people will report crimes to the police keeping us all safer. Hayden was also a leader in ensuring U and T visa (special visas for human trafficking and domestic violence survivors) certification reforms were practical and included in the Protect Act. The process will be faster, more consistent and the reforms have been lauded by non-profits dedicated to ending sexual exploitation and abuse.

Finally, I want to say Kevin, unlike his predecessor, has the immense respect of his fellow district attorneys. Kevin was elected by his peers to lead the Massachusetts Association of

District Attorneys. In that role Kevin leads monthly meetings about criminal justice reforms policies and trends. He is a statewide leader and voice for all justice-minded prosecutors.

There is a long list of why Kevin’s opponents are not the kind district attorneys we need. Both have continued distracting controversies. Rollins displays hers on a daily basis on social media. Champion, in a demonstration of thin-skinned vindictiveness, recently filed a lawsuit against the Globe for $50,000 because she was “defamed” by a Globe story discussing where she lived. And, yes, Hayden was fined for campaign missteps while running for district attorney. But the difference between Hayden and his opponents is that he paid the fine and it no longer serves as distraction. He also has not made the mistake again. Essentially, the “buck” and the controversy stopped with him.

In conclusion, I am asking you, the voters of Suffolk County, to vote for Kevin Hayden on September 1. If what I described above is new to you, it’s because Kevin was focused on the work and not on politics or marketing. Kevin is a public servant that has earned your trust and your vote.

Lydia Edwards is a Massachusetts State Senator representing the Third Suffolk District which includes Revere.

news_revere.title: Gov. Healey does the right thing to ban kratom
news_revere.author: Journal Staff
news_revere.summary:
Gov. Healey does the

right thing to ban kratom

The decision last week by Gov. Maura Healey and the Mass. Dept. of Public Health to issue an order classifying kratom as a Schedule 1 drug, thereby effectively banning the sale of kratom products, removes a dangerous and highly-addictive substance from store shelves in our state.

Kratom is derived from the leaves of a tree in Southeast Asia, where it has been used medicinally in its natural form for hundreds of years with a low degree of dependency when used in moderation.

However, in this country, kratom products flooding convenience and other stores bear little resemblance to that traditional herb. Instead, manufacturers are distributing highly-potent extract powders, tablets, and gummies that isolate and concentrate kratom’s active alkaloid, 7-hydroxymitragynine (7-OH).

Because these commercial products have been completely unregulated, consumers have had no way of knowing the dosage or chemical purity of what they are ingesting. It is these hyper-concentrated products that lead rapidly to dependency, severe withdrawal, and an elevated risk of overdose—especially among curious children and teenagers.

A number of cities and towns across the state, most recently Revere, already have taken matters into their own hands by banning the sale of kratom products in their communities.

However, local ordinances create a patchwork defense that allows buyers to simply drive to the next town over. Governor Healey’s sweeping statewide ban establishes a uniform line of defense, ensuring that these unpredictable and hazardous products can no longer target the health and safety of our youth anywhere in the Commonwealth.

Iran is holding all the cards

When the United States and Israel embarked on their war against Iran almost six months ago, the ease with which they accomplished the assassination of the Iranian leaders created the narrative of a quick end to the hostilities.

Israeli intelligence had convinced American leaders that the regime would fall if Iran’s top leaders were removed and that the successor leadership would cave in swiftly to demands to end Iran’s nuclear weapons program.

Six weeks into the conflict, we were told by our leaders that Iran had “no cards.”

But now, six months later, it is clear that Iran holds all the cards.

The U.S. has no answer militarily to the Iranians’ ongoing blockade of the Strait of Hormuz. Despite months of bombing of Iranian military (and some civilian) targets by the U.S. and the Israelis, the Iranians’ drones continue to pose a serious threat both to the critical infrastructure of other countries and American military bases in the region.

Moreover, the war has drained the U.S. military of its weaponry, leaving our military

critically short of both offensive and defensive missiles that will take years to replenish.

The war also is draining the morale of our service members, who are living under strenuous conditions of long deployments while under the constant threat of attack with no clear mission.

In addition, the war has created ever-widening fissures not only between the U.S. and Israel, but also between the U.S. and its allies both in the region and around the world, none of whom were consulted before the U.S. started the war.

Instead of displaying our military prowess, the war has demonstrated that the U.S. is a feckless, unreliable, and unhinged partner of limited capacity who is the new rogue actor on the world stage.

By contrast, Iran has strengthened its alliances with Russia and China, with the Chinese buying Iranian oil, and the Russians supplying Iran with weapons and crucial logistical support that helps to target U.S. military installations.

The U.S. also has failed at the negotiation table. The so-called U.S. negotiating team of Kushner, Witfkoff, and Vance has zero experience dealing with either the Iranians, the intricacies of a nuclear weapons program, or how to negotiate in a war-time setting. It was their simplistic Memorandum of Understanding 60 days ago that led the Iranians to believe that they can control the strait.

With the U.S. and the world economy straining under the burden of higher energy prices — with no end in sight — it is becoming increasingly clear that the only option for the U.S. to get out of this quagmire is to declare victory and go home — and let the proverbial chips fall where they may.

news_revere.title: Election 2026: A Primary Primer
news_revere.author: Jim Mitchell
news_revere.summary:
The Sept. 1 State Primary Election is still two weeks and four days away. But Early/Absentee Ballots are already in the mail to Saugus residents who request them so they can vote early

 

By Mark E. Vogler

 

If you are a registered Democrat in Saugus, you should have at least three major reasons for voting in the Sept. 1 state Primary Election. The major one would be to choose between incumbent U.S. Sen. Edward J. Markey or his challenger, U.S. Rep. Seth Moulton. The second reason would be to pick from the six candidates who are seeking to fill Moulton’s vacant congressional seat. Your third reason is the District 6 Governor’s Council race. Terrence W. Kennedy, of Lynnfield, who has served since 2011, faces a challenger – Diann Mary Baylis, an immigration attorney of Marblehead. Right now, the winner faces no Republican opposition in November unless a candidate mounts a write-in campaign.

You have a fourth reason if you are a Democrat registered to vote in Precincts 1, 2 or 4 through 9 – picking between two Lynn residents – Lynn City Councilor Peter Meaney and Lynn’s Inspectional Division Director, Zosia Jean VanMeter, for the right to challenge longtime state Rep. Donald Wong (R-Saugus) in the Nov. 3 state General Election. Wong, who seeks a ninth term, has no primary opponent – but will face his first political opponent in four elections after his uncontested victories in 2024, 2022 and 2020.

If you are a registered Republican in Saugus, regardless of the precinct, your major reason for voting will be to help decide between two candidates to represent your party in the Nov. 3 General Election against Gov. Maura Healey, who seeks her second four-year term in this year’s gubernatorial race. Michael Roger Minogue of Hamilton is running against Brian Shortsleeve of Barnstable. Minogue, the former CEO of Abiomed, received the landslide endorsement for governor at the Republican Party’s State Convention back in April, with 70 percent of the votes. Shortsleeve, who ran the MBTA under former Gov. Charlie Baker, drew about 16 percent of the votes to earn a spot on the ballot. This is the only Republican race on a Saugus election ballot that will matter on Sept. 1.

There is a paucity of candidates for office in this year’s primary, especially for the Republican Party. If you are voting in the precincts that are part of the Ninth Essex House District (Precincts 1, 2 and 4 through 9), you won’t have a candidate to vote for for six public offices: Secretary of State, State Auditor, the 6th District Governor’s Council seat, the Third Essex Senate seat, the Essex County District Attorney and the Essex County Register of Probate.

If you are voting in Precincts 3 or 10 – which are part of the 16th District House District – you will not be voting for a candidate for seven offices. There are no Republican candidates running for the 16th Suffolk House seat.

John Deaton, the only Republican candidate for the U.S. Senate seat held by Markey, will be on the Nov. 3 ballot. Deaton is already battle-tested. He ran against U.S. Sen. Elizabeth Warren in the general election two years ago and lost by about 20 points. Micah Quinney Jones, a decorated U.S. Army veteran and attorney from Essex, will face off in November against the winner of the six Democrats aspiring to win Moulton’s congressional seat. Other Republican candidates who will be on the November ballot are Shawn Oliver, a New Bedford city councilor, for Lieutenant Governor; Michael C. Walsh, a Lynnfield attorney, for Attorney General; and Elizabeth Dionne, a former Belmonte Select Board member, for Treasurer. Wong, the longtime popular Republican legislator, will be on the ballot for eight of the 10 Saugus precincts.

The Democratic Party has candidates running for all offices. But Gov. Healey, Lt. Gov. Kimberly Driscoll, Attorney General Andrea Joy Cambell, Secretary of State William Francis Galvin, Treasurer Deborah B. Goldberg, State Auditor Diana DiZoglio, State Sen. Peter Crighton, state Rep. Jessica Ann Giannino (the Revere Democrat who represents Precincts 3 and 10 in Saugus), District Attorney Paul Tucker and Register of Probate Pamela Casey O’Brien have no primary opposition and will all move on to the November General Election. Two members of the Saugus legislative delegation – Sen. Crighton, a state senator since 2018, and Giannino, who has been a state representative since 2020 — are positioned to go uncontested again in their respective reelection campaigns. Neither legislator has faced Republican opposition since being elected. Galvin, DiZoglio, Tucker and O’Brien face no opposition from Republicans in November.

Meanwhile, registered Democratic voters will have to do some research to determine their choice to replace Congressman Moulton for the Massachusetts Sixth Congressional District seat. The Democratic candidates are Bethany Andres-Beck of Middleton; John A. Beccia III, of Lynnfield; Jamie M. Belsito, of Topsfield; Dan Koh, of Andover; Mariah L. Lancaster, of Salem; and Tram T. Nguyen, of Andover.

 

Who can vote

As of Aug. 1, there were 22,794 registered voters in Saugus, according to information provided by the Town Clerk’s Office in Saugus. About 69 percent (15,700) are unenrolled voters. They can still vote by designating themselves Democratic or Republican Party affiliation before casting their votes. There are 4,685 registered Democrats in Saugus – about 21 percent of the total voters. There are 2,172 registered Republicans in Saugus – about 10 percent of the total voters. There are 86 registered members of the United Independent Party, about .38 of 1 percent. The next highest party affiliation is Libertarian – with 57 registered, about a quarter of 1 percent. Other party affiliations include Conservative, Pizza Party, Twelve Visions Party, Green Party USA, We The People, Green Rainbow, Constitution Party, Mass. Independent Party, Socialist, Inter 3rd Party, Pirate, Working Families.

 

How you can vote early

The overwhelming majority of registered voters in Saugus will vote on Primary Day, based on historical information. But every registered voter has the option to vote by mail if they want. All registered voters in the state should have received a “Vote by Mail Application” with a postage free postcard to mail to the Town or City Clerk’s Office. The deadline to mail back the application to receive a mail-in ballot is 5 p.m. on Aug. 25. To receive a primary ballot, the voter must select Democratic or Republican on the postcard. Voting by mail-in ballot in a primary will not enroll you in a political party.

Saugus Town Clerk Ellen Schena said the Early Voting Card return as of Tuesday (Aug. 11) morning was 2,241 – 1,671 Democratic Party and 570 Republican Party for the upcoming primary. “At the same exact time 2 years ago in 2024 the count for mail in EV ballots was as follows: 3034 (1969 Dem & 904 Rep). So over 800 less,” Schena told The Saugus Advocate this week.

Registered voters also have the option to participate early, in person if they are concerned that they may not be able to vote on Primary Election Day. In-Person Early Voting for the Sept. 1 State Primary Election will begin on Saturday, Aug. 22, from 9:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. in the Community Room of the Saugus Public Library, at 295 Central St. Voters should enter through the Taylor Street Entrance. This is also the last day to register to vote in the election.

In-Person Early Voting will be held for five additional days, as follows:

  • Monday, August 24, 2026 – 8:30 a.m. to 7:00 p.m.
  • Tuesday, August 25, 2026 – 8:15 a.m. to 4:00 p.m.
  • Wednesday, August 26, 2026 – 8:15 a.m. to 4:00 p.m.
  • Thursday, August 27, 2026 – 8:15 a.m. to 4:00 p.m.
  • Friday, August 28, 2026 – 8:15 a.m. to 12:30 p.m.

 

Where to vote in Saugus on Election Day

Most of Saugus’ registered voters in the town’s 10 precincts who will cast their ballots in the state Primary Election will go to six different polling locations on Tuesday, Sept. 1. The polls will be open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. that day.

If you are a registered voter and don’t know where you can vote, please call the Town Clerk’s Office between today (Friday) and next Tuesday at 781-231-4101 or 781-231-4102 or drop by Town Hall if you are near Saugus Center and request to see the Street List, which lists all town residents broken down by precincts and according to the streets where they live.

Here are the current polling locations:

Precinct          Polling Location

1 and 9            Saugus Middle/High School Complex,1 Pearce Memorial Dr.

2 and 6            Veteran’s Early Learning Center, 39 Hurd Ave.

3 and 5            Saugus Senior Center, 466 Central St.

4 and 8            Belmonte STEAM Academy, 25 Dow St.

7                      Knight of Columbus, 57 Appleton St.

10                    Italian American Club, 1 Beachview Ave.

news_communities.title: Man posed as ex-roommate to vote illegally, then reported him, feds say
news_communities.author: Asher Klein
news_communities.summary:
A Chinese man living in Massachusetts impersonated his former roommate, also a Chinese national, to illegally vote on his behalf, then anonymously reported the former roommate to immigration authorities, federal prosecutors said Wednesday.

The apparent revenge scheme — the former roommates ended up with dueling claims in court, according to a criminal complaint — nearly got the former roommate and his wife deported, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office for Massachusetts.

Yupeng Sun, 33, was arrested on Wednesday on charges of fraudulent voter registration and fraudulent voting, prosecutors said. He was due in federal court in Boston; it wasn’t immediately clear if he had an attorney who could speak to the charge.

According to the criminal complaint, Sun allegedly admitted to investigators last month that he “used his name to vote,” referring to the former roommate, whom he’d confirmed he still had “very, very” bad feelings towards. Sun later texted law enforcement to say he understood it was likely he’d be charged but that he’d been wrongfully arrested and charged because of the man.

The complaint says that Sun rented a room with a Chinese family in Malden from 2021 until May 2023, when Sun was arrested on an assault and battery charge involving the adult daughter of the man he’d later allegedly impersonate. The charges were dismissed over a year later, but Sun claimed in court he’d been unlawfully evicted.

The next year, the man and his wife had forms submitted in their names seeking to give up legal permanent resident status — their green cards. And when they flew back to the U.S. from a trip abroad, they were taken into custody at Logan airport and had the deportation process begun, according to the complaint.

That October, ahead of the presidential election, the man — he wasn’t named in the criminal complaint to protect his and his family’s privacy — had a voter registration application submitted, and an early voting ballot was cast in his name.

Over a year later, the federal agency Homeland Security Investigations began getting tips both online and by mail about the Malden man voting as a non-citizen.

In the meantime, the man and his wife had successfully petitioned the Boston Immigration Court to restore their green cards — they’d testified about their former roommate having access to personal information because he’d helped them apply for insurance, according to the complaint. And when investigators asked him about illegally voting, he said it was possibly Sun who did it to retaliate for his arrest.

If he’s convicted, Sun faces up to five years in prison and a $250,000 fine, prosecutors said.

news_communities.title: NeighborHealth promotes safe summer riding through its Annual Children’s Bike Safety Day
news_communities.author: admin
news_communities.summary:
Families gathered at the East Boston Farmers Market during National Farmer’s Market Week for an afternoon of bike safety education, helmet fittings and community fun

BOSTON, MA (August 7, 2026) – NeighborHealth hosted its annual Children’s Bike Safety Day at the East Boston Farmers Market earlier this week, bringing together local families for an afternoon focused on bike safety, healthy outdoor activity and community connection. With support from Boston Children’s Hospital, the event provided free bike helmets, professional helmet fittings and bike safety education to help children ride safely throughout the summer and beyond.

Designed to promote safe cycling habits and active lifestyles, the event gave families the opportunity to learn about proper helmet use and other important safety practices, all during a special celebration of National Farmers Market Week, offering special activities that highlight the important role local farmer’s play in expanding access to fresh food. Both the bike safety event and Farmer’s Market Week celebration reflect NeighborHealth’s commitment to supporting the health and well-being of children both inside and outside the clinical setting.

The highlight of the event was a bike raffle that awarded six children brand-new bicycles, donated by Boston Children’s Hospital, Excel Academy and First Priority Credit Union. Families were also invited to visit the bike safety tent, where staff from Boston Children’s Hospital provided helmet fittings and shared information about safe riding practices.

“This is truly one of my favorite events of the year,” said Julio Mazul, MD, Executive Vice President and Chief Medical Officer. “There’s nothing quite like seeing a child’s face light up when they hear their name called and realize they’ve just won a new bike. We want every child to experience the fun and freedom that comes with riding a bike, and we’re proud to partner with Boston Children’s Hospital to help ensure families have the equipment and knowledge they need to ride safely all summer long.”

Through its injury prevention efforts, Boston Children’s Hospital provides families with practical safety resources that help reduce the risk of preventable injuries.

“Parents have a lot on their plates, so when we can bring these resources directly into the community, we make it that much easier for families to access them,” said Barbara DiGirolamo, M.Ed., CPSTI, Injury Prevention Program Coordinator at Boston Children’s Hospital. “Whether it’s helping a child find the right helmet fit or answering a parent’s questions about safe riding, these conversations can have a lasting impact.”

Children’s Bike Safety Day was held as part of NeighborHealth’s East Boston Farmers Market, which brings together fresh food vendors, community organizations, health resources and family-focused programming throughout the season. The annual event highlights the power of community partnerships in creating opportunities for children and families to stay healthy, active and connected.

NeighborHealth’s East Boston Farmers Market is held Wednesdays from 3:00 to 6:30 pm, July 8th through October 28th (October hours 3:00–6:00 pm) at Central Square Park in East Boston. This vibrant market, led by Market Manager Kelsey Briggs, attracts hundreds of families weekly and hosts a diverse array of produce and prepared food vendors alongside numerous community essential services and children’s programing.

The market accommodates cash, debit, credit cards, and app payments, and also accepts WIC coupons, Senior coupons, SNAP/food stamps/EBT, P-EBT, and City of Boston Farmers Market coupons, which are available to eligible Boston residents in need of food assistance at the Community Resource Center at 282 Meridian St, East Boston.

For more information about NeighborHealth’s East Boston Farmers Market visit: www.neighborhealth.com.
